conceptTag: A snack brand: supermarkets or online?
readerTitle: Your snack sells for $4. Where should it be sold?
caseNote: 적용 레슨 · 가상 사례 (스낵 브랜드, 청소 서비스) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 채널은 '얼마를 떼어 가나'가 아니라 '그 몫으로 무엇을 사 주고, 내 상품이 그 채널에 맞는가'로 고른다.
misconception: 중간 유통을 빼고 직접 팔면 유통 마진만큼 그대로 더 남는다.

sources.text: 유통 채널 마진과 채널 적합성에 관한 표준 마케팅 개념

factChecks.note: 손익 비교: 온라인 n박스 누적 15.40n − 20, 같은 봉지 수의 슈퍼마켓 누적 12n × $1.00 = 12n. 15.40n − 20 > 12n → n > 5.88, 즉 6번째 박스부터 온라인이 앞섭니다. 6박스: 온라인 $72.40 vs 슈퍼마켓 $72.00.
청소 서비스(가상): 방문당 $120 − 인건비·자재 $80 = $40. 플랫폼 수수료 20% = $24 → 남는 돈 $16. 격주 방문 연 26회 × $24 = 연 $624.
입점비(slotting fee), 브랜드가 부담하는 판촉 할인, 미판매 재고, 대금 지급 지연은 식품 소매에서 흔히 거론되는 비용이지만 수치는 넣지 않았습니다. 나라·체인별로 다르므로 일반적 표현만 유지하세요.

cards.title: Your snack sells for $4. Where should it be sold?
body: You make spiced chickpea crisps. In the supermarket they sit on the shelf at $4 a bag. After the store and the distributor take their share, you get $2.20.
A friend says: "Sell online and keep the whole $4." It sounds obvious. The numbers say otherwise.

image.label: A snack bag on a supermarket shelf next to a shipping box
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 왼쪽은 슈퍼마켓 선반 위 병아리콩 스낵 봉지($4 가격표), 오른쪽은 같은 봉지 12개가 든 배송 박스. 가운데 갈림길 화살표. 실제 브랜드·매장 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which channel leaves you more money?
body: Supermarket: each bag leaves you $1.00 after the store, distributor and making costs.
Online: you sell a 12-bag box for $40. You pay for packing, shipping and ads to win each new customer.

options.text: Online, because nobody takes a cut
options.feedback: No middleman, but shipping, fees and ads replace their cut. This is **middlemen and their margins** at work: removing the middleman doesn't remove the work they did.

options.text: The supermarket, because its cut is a fair price
options.feedback: Often true for a cheap, impulse snack. But it ignores fans who buy again and again, where online can win.

options.text: It depends on how many boxes an online customer buys
options.feedback: Right. Online pays for itself only through repeat orders. The next cards show where the line falls.

cards.title: One bag through the supermarket
body: Small per bag, but the store brings the shoppers. You pay nothing to find them.

cards.title: One box sold online
body: A $40 box of 12 bags costs $14.40 to make, $9 to pack and ship, and $1.20 in card fees. That leaves **$15.40**, about $1.28 a bag. Better than the shelf.
But winning a new customer with ads costs about $20. The first box loses $4.60. Compared with selling the same bags in stores, a customer must buy **six boxes** before online comes out ahead.

image.label: A staircase of six boxes crossing a line
image.brief: 박스 6개가 계단처럼 쌓이고, 점선으로 된 '슈퍼마켓 수익선'을 6번째 박스에서 넘는 그래프형 일러스트. 첫 박스는 빨간색(−$4.60), 나머지는 초록색.

cards.title: Middlemen and their margins
body: The supermarket's $1.40 isn't a tax. It buys shelf space, foot traffic, cold storage and the shopper who grabs your bag on the way to the checkout.
Going direct means doing all of that yourself. Ask what a middleman's cut pays for, and what it would cost you to replace it.
cards.softwareNote: App stores and marketplaces take a share of each sale. Skipping them saves the fee but means paying to be found some other way.

cards.title: Channel fit
body: A $4 snack is cheap, bought on impulse and bought with other groceries. That fits a supermarket. Few people plan an online order for one bag of crisps.

Online fits a different buyer: the fan who eats a bag a day, the office stocking a kitchen, the person sending a gift. The **channel fit** question is which buyer you're serving, not which channel is better.

image.label: Two shoppers: impulse buyer and loyal fan
image.brief: 왼쪽은 장바구니를 든 채 계산대 앞에서 스낵을 집는 사람, 오른쪽은 문 앞에서 정기 배송 박스를 받는 사람. 각각 'Supermarket'과 'Online' 라벨. 로고 없음.

cards.title: The shelf has hidden costs too.
body: Supermarkets may charge fees to stock new products, expect you to fund discounts, send back stock that doesn't sell and pay weeks later.
So the $1.00 a bag can shrink. Run both paths with every cost included before you choose. Many brands start small in both and let the numbers decide.

cards.title: Now it's a cleaning business.
body: Your regulars book a clean every two weeks at $120. Each visit leaves $40 after cleaner pay and supplies.
A booking platform can bring new customers. It takes 20% of every job booked through it, repeats included.

options.text: Join and send all bookings through it
options.feedback: You fill your calendar, but each visit leaves $16 instead of $40. For a regular, that's $624 a year in fees. The **middleman's margin** repeats on work you'd have kept anyway.

options.text: Use it to fill empty slots, and win regulars through referrals and local channels
options.feedback: The platform fits one-off and new customers; your own channels fit the regulars. That's **channel fit** and margin thinking together.
You keep the full $40, but empty slots earn nothing. The platform's cut buys customers you can't reach yet.

cards.title: A channel's cut is a price. Ask what it buys.
body: You used two ideas: **middlemen and their margins** (what the cut pays for) and **channel fit** (which buyer each channel suits).
**Try it today:** pick one channel you sell through. Write what it costs you per sale, and what you'd spend to do its job yourself.
